- allow competing regional priorities to be considered together;
- strengthen transparency and auditability; and
- clarify the distinction between political advocacy and public financial administration.

The proposed resolution in section 2 is therefore recommended for adoption.

---

### Suggested covering note

> Colleagues,  
>
> I am circulating the attached discussion paper for consideration. It proposes the dissolution of the Members’ Initiative Pool and the transfer of its uncommitted balance to the Assembly’s general appropriation.  
>
> The proposal is concerned with institutional accountability and the appropriate administration of public funds, rather than with the merits of individual projects previously supported by the Pool. I would welcome factual corrections, particularly concerning the Pool’s legal basis, current balance, outstanding commitments and applicable financial procedures.  
>
> This paper is circulated in my professional/personal capacity and should not be taken as representing the position of the Research Library or the Assembly unless formally authorised.

# Plan to Build and Protect an Owned Live-Events Rights Portfolio

## 1. Define the rights thesis

The objective should not simply be to buy airtime. It should be to create a recurring, recognisable live-event property that your organisation controls at the **event, media-rights, brand, data and commercial levels**.

Prioritise properties with:

- A strong live-viewing proposition
- Predictable annual or seasonal scheduling
- A clear audience gap
- Limited existing rights competition
- Expandability into multiple territories and platforms
- Distinctive rules, venues, talent or presentation
- Sponsorship and licensing potential beyond advertising

A practical portfolio might combine:

1. **One flagship property** — the marquee event or league.
2. **Several supporting events** — regular fixtures that fill the calendar.
3. **A development tier** — youth, women’s, regional or amateur competitions.
4. **Ancillary content** — documentaries, behind-the-scenes access, analysis, highlights and digital formats.

The flagship should be capable of becoming a cultural appointment, rather than merely another event on the schedule.

---

## 2. Choose the ownership model

There are three broad structures.

### A. Fully owned event

Your company creates, promotes and operates the event itself.

**Advantages**
- Maximum control
- Strongest chain of title
- Greater freedom over rules, scheduling, format and exploitation
- Long-term enterprise value

**Disadvantages**
- Highest operational and financial risk
- You bear responsibility for venues, participants, insurance, safety and production

### B. Joint venture

You form a separate event company with a federation, promoter, venue group, investor or talent partner.

**Advantages**
- Shared capital and expertise
- Easier access to participants, venues or regulatory approval
- Potentially faster launch

**Disadvantages**
- Governance disputes
- Co-owner approval rights
- More difficult future sale or sublicensing

### C. Commissioned property under exclusive licence

A third party creates or operates the event, while your company receives exclusive rights for a defined term.

**Advantages**
- Lower operational exposure
- Faster to launch
- Access to established expertise

**Disadvantages**
- You may not truly own the property
- Renewal and change-of-control risks
- Greater risk of rights leakage or competing events

For the flagship property, the preferred structure is generally either **full ownership through a dedicated subsidiary** or a **joint venture in which your company has decisive control and a robust buyout mechanism**.

---

## 3. Create a dedicated rights-holding entity

Use a ring-fenced subsidiary or event group to hold the portfolio.

That entity should own or control:

- Event names and trademarks
- Logos and visual identity
- Rules and competition format
- Websites, apps and social accounts
- Audio-visual recordings
- Production assets
- Event data and statistics
- Sponsorship and licensing rights
- Contracts with participants, venues and suppliers
- Archives and historical footage
- International rights

The parent news organisation can then hold an exclusive licence from the rights-holding entity, while preserving the ability to:

- Sell or sublicense rights to third parties
- Bring in investment
- Acquire complementary properties
- Separate editorial operations from commercial rights activity
- Sell part of the portfolio without selling the core news business

Maintain a formal **chain-of-title file** from the outset. Every material creative, commercial and operational right should be traceable to a signed agreement.

---

## 4. Design a genuinely protectable event property

An event becomes valuable when it is distinctive and repeatable.

Develop a formal property bible covering:

- Name and marks
- Competition rules
- Qualification and participation system
- Fixture structure
- Venue standards
- Timing and broadcast windows
- Scoring or ranking system
- Presentation style
- Official music, graphics and visual language
- Ceremonies and rituals
- Safety and integrity procedures
- Sponsorship categories
- Digital extensions
- Archive and data policy

Do not rely solely on copyright in the rules or format. In many jurisdictions, ideas, rules and sporting formats receive limited protection. Protection should instead be layered through:

- Trademark registration
- Copyright in graphics, films, manuals and software
- Contractual confidentiality
- Exclusive participant and venue agreements
- Database rights where available
- Passing-off or unfair-competition remedies
- Access controls and accreditation rules
- Strong brand recognition and first-mover advantage

Before committing to a name, conduct trademark and domain searches in every commercially relevant territory.

---

## 5. Secure the underlying event rights

The event rights agreement should be broader than a conventional television deal. It should expressly cover, as applicable:

### Media rights
- Live linear television
- Streaming and OTT
- Mobile and connected devices
- Pay, free-to-air and subscription services
- Highlights and clips
- Delayed and catch-up viewing
- Radio and audio
- Social and short-form video
- Virtual and augmented reality
- In-flight, out-of-home and venue screenings
- Gaming and simulation uses

### Geographic rights
- Domestic territory
- International territories
- Inbound and outbound digital access
- Territorial blackouts and geo-blocking

### Time rights
- Live
- Near-live
- Delayed
- Catch-up
- Archive
- Perpetual historical use, if obtainable

### Commercial rights
- Sponsorship
- Naming rights
- Advertising inventory
- Betting and fantasy integrations, subject to law
- Merchandising
- Licensing
- Hospitality
- Ticketing
- NFTs or other digital products, where commercially and legally appropriate

### Data rights
- Official statistics
- Timing and tracking data
- Metadata
- Betting data
- Data feeds for apps and third parties
- Artificial-intelligence and machine-learning uses, if relevant

The agreement should state that rights are granted **exclusively**, not merely on a “first call” or preferred basis.

---

## 6. Contract with every rights-bearing stakeholder

A common failure is securing the promoter’s agreement while leaving other rights unaddressed.

Conduct a rights audit covering:

- Event organiser or federation
- Participants and teams
- Athletes’ image, likeness and performance rights
- Coaches, officials and commentators
- Venues and venue owners
- Local authorities
- Music and entertainment performers
- Production crews
- Photographers and freelance contributors
- Data providers
- Sponsors
- Security and access-control providers
- Relevant regulators

Participant agreements should include, subject to local law:

- Permission to record and broadcast performances
- Name, image and likeness rights
- Promotional use
- Archive use
- Social clips and highlights
- International exploitation
- Consent to reasonable edits and commentary
- Restrictions on unauthorised live streaming
- Confidentiality and embargoes
- Integrity and anti-corruption obligations
- Availability and non-compete provisions during the event window

Use specific, legally compliant releases rather than assuming that attendance or participation gives the broadcaster all necessary rights.

---

## 7. Lock in exclusivity carefully

Exclusivity should be defined by **right, platform, territory, language, time window and exploitation type**.

For example:

- Exclusive live domestic television rights
- Exclusive domestic streaming rights
- Exclusive official highlights for a defined period
- Exclusive official data rights
- Exclusive international distribution rights
- Exclusive archive and documentary access

Avoid vague wording such as “exclusive broadcast rights” without defining whether that includes clips, social media, foreign feeds, venues, mobile services and user-generated content.

Include:

- No competing event during protected dates
- No parallel or “shadow” competition
- No unauthorised camera or stream access
- Restrictions on participants’ personal live streams
- Clear rules for press access and news reporting
- Limited, legally required news-access exceptions
- A consent process for third-party sublicensing
- Remedies for rights leakage

Exclusivity must be drafted consistently with applicable competition, media, sporting and public-access laws. A rights strategy should not be designed around unlawfully blocking legitimate news reporting or creating an impermissible market foreclosure.

---

## 8. Build a multi-year term with control rights

A flagship should normally have enough runway to justify investment. Consider:

- Initial term of five to ten years
- Extension options tied to performance milestones
- Renewal rights at your election
- First negotiation or matching rights for future editions
- Approval rights over format changes
- Approval rights over competing events
- Step-in rights if the promoter fails
- Termination rights for integrity, insolvency, safety or regulatory failures
- Buyout rights over key partners
- Change-of-control protections
- Assignment and sublicensing rights

Avoid an arrangement where the event operator can freely sell the next cycle to a competitor after your launch investment has built the brand.

If working with a federation or promoter, negotiate a **reversion or buyout formula** so that you can acquire full control after reaching agreed audience, revenue or investment thresholds.

---

## 9. Establish production and technical control

Owning rights without controlling the feed can still leave you vulnerable.

Your operating model should provide for:

- Your appointed host broadcaster or production partner
- Ownership or perpetual licence of the master recordings
- Access to all clean feeds and camera angles
- Redundant transmission paths
- Disaster-recovery facilities
- Central rights-management and scheduling systems
- Digital watermarking and forensic monitoring
- Secure credentials and contributor access
- Geo-blocking and device controls
- Rapid takedown processes
- A complete event archive

The contract should prevent the event operator or production supplier from retaining the ability to reuse footage, create a competing feed or license clips independently.

Set technical standards in advance for:

- Resolution and frame rate
- Audio and commentary feeds
- Captioning and accessibility
- Latency
- Metadata
- Replay and archive delivery
- Ad-insertion capability
- International versioning

---

## 10. Create a strong calendar and distribution strategy

The event should support the economics of a channel rather than compete with them.

Build a calendar with:

- A predictable annual championship or final
- Regular qualifying or league fixtures
- Shoulder programming
- Replays and analysis
- Short-form and social content
- Documentary and human-interest material
- Off-season events or development competitions

Use the flagship to drive:

- Linear audience
- Streaming registration
- Subscription conversion
- Sponsorship packages
- News coverage
- Community participation
- Email and first-party data
- International distribution

Do not automatically retain every right exclusively. A carefully selected sublicense can increase reach, establish legitimacy and create a higher benchmark for future valuations. Retain the rights most important to audience acquisition and strategic control.

---

## 11. Make the commercial case before launch

Prepare a five-year rights and event model covering:

### Costs
- Prize money or participant fees
- Venue hire
- Insurance
- Sanctioning and regulatory costs
- Production
- Transmission
- Marketing
- Staffing
- Security and medical provision
- Legal and rights clearance
- Technology
- Contingency
- Minimum guarantees

### Revenue
- Advertising
- Sponsorship
- Naming rights
- Subscriptions
- Pay-per-view
- Ticketing
- Hospitality
- International sublicensing
- Merchandise
- Licensing
- Data
- Platform partnerships

Model at least three scenarios:

1. Base case
2. High-growth case
3. Adverse case involving low audiences, cancellation or a legal dispute

Set investment gates. For example:

- Pilot approval
- First season approval
- Renewal approval
- Expansion approval
- International exploitation approval

A flagship should not depend on optimistic advertising forecasts alone. Secure anchor sponsors and distribution commitments where possible, but avoid giving sponsors or platforms rights that undermine your long-term exclusivity.

---

## 12. Pilot before scaling

Use a pilot or inaugural event to test:

- Audience demand
- Event format
- Venue suitability
- Production workflow
- Participant quality
- Sponsorship value
- Technical delivery
- Regulatory exposure
- Rights enforcement
- Social and streaming performance

The pilot agreement should already contain the long-term rights architecture. Do not run a successful pilot under loose terms and then discover that the operator, venue or participants control the valuable rights.

Measure:

- Live reach
- Average minute audience
- Completion rate
- Streaming concurrency
- Viewer acquisition cost
- Repeat viewing
- Sponsor impressions
- Social engagement
- Earned media
- Conversion to owned platforms
- Cost per viewer hour
- Revenue per viewer hour

---

## 13. Protect the brand and enforce the rights

Create a dedicated rights-protection programme with:

- Trademark watching
- Domain monitoring
- Social-platform monitoring
- Automated stream detection
- Notice-and-takedown templates
- Platform escalation contacts
- Local enforcement counsel
- Evidence-preservation procedures
- Anti-counterfeit and ticketing controls
- Accreditation and camera-access rules
- Contractual penalties for unauthorised exploitation

Maintain a written enforcement policy distinguishing:

- Genuine piracy
- Unauthorised commercial exploitation
- Permitted news reporting
- User-generated commentary
- Fair dealing or fair use
- Legitimate criticism and public-interest coverage

This is particularly important for a news organisation, whose editorial operations must remain able to report on the event independently and lawfully.

---

## 14. Separate editorial integrity from commercial control

Because you operate a news channel, establish governance safeguards:

- Separate commercial rights and editorial management
- Publish an editorial policy for coverage of owned events
- Disclose material ownership interests where appropriate
- Maintain independent editorial commissioning
- Avoid using news coverage solely as disguised promotion
- Establish conflict-of-interest procedures
- Give journalists appropriate access without compromising the rights business
- Separate sponsor influence from editorial decisions

This protects both the credibility of the channel and the long-term value of the property.

---

## 15. Suggested implementation timetable

### Months 0–3: Strategy and diligence
- Audience and competitor analysis
- Rights-gap mapping
- Candidate event shortlist
- Legal and regulatory review
- Preliminary economics
- Ownership and governance design

### Months 3–6: Property creation
- Name and format development
- Trademark clearance
- Venue and participant negotiations
- Draft rights architecture
- Pilot budget
- Sponsorship prospectus
- Production and safety planning

### Months 6–12: Contracting and pilot
- Execute stakeholder agreements
- Establish event subsidiary
- Secure insurance and approvals
- Produce pilot
- Deploy rights monitoring
- Evaluate audience and commercial results

### Year 2: Launch and consolidation
- Run a recurring season
- Expand distribution
- Secure multi-year sponsors
- Build archive and data products
- Strengthen participant and venue exclusivity
- Begin international sales

### Years 3–5: Portfolio expansion
- Add complementary events
- Acquire or invest in adjacent properties
- Develop women’s, youth or regional tiers
- Build international formats
- Consider a dedicated streaming product
- Refinance or partially monetise the portfolio without surrendering strategic control

## 16. Core documents to commission

Have specialist counsel prepare, at minimum:

1. Rights-acquisition or event-creation agreement  
2. Participant and team agreements  
3. Venue agreement  
4. Production and host-broadcast agreement  
5. Distribution and sublicensing template  
6. Sponsor and naming-rights agreement  
7. Data and statistics agreement  
8. Trademark and IP schedule  
9. Event rules and competition regulations  
10. Safety, integrity and anti-corruption code  
11. Platform and piracy-enforcement protocol  
12. Privacy, consent and image-rights notices  
13. Insurance and indemnity schedule  
14. Editorial-commercial separation policy  
15. Contingency, cancellation and force-majeure plan

## Strategic bottom line

The strongest route is to create a **dedicated, repeatable event property**, hold the core IP and recordings in a controlled subsidiary, secure comprehensive exclusive rights from every relevant stakeholder, and build enough calendar depth that the property becomes difficult for audiences, sponsors and distributors to replace.

The key is to protect more than the live feed. You want control over the **brand, format, participants, venues, archive, data, digital extensions, sponsorship inventory and future editions**. Engage local media, sports, competition, IP, employment, privacy and regulatory counsel before signing any commitment, because the enforceability and scope of exclusivity will depend heavily on the jurisdiction and the particular sport or event.

A good demo yard should be designed as a **small operating farm plus a controlled customer facility**, not merely a large parking area. Build it in phases so you can start hosting buyers before every hectare is fully developed.

## 1. Establish the design brief first

Before moving soil, document:

- Largest and heaviest machines you will demonstrate
- Tractor horsepower and turning-circle requirements
- Implements requiring plowing, cultivating, drilling, mowing, hauling, or loading
- Whether customers will merely watch or operate machines
- Expected visitor numbers and event sizes
- Hours of operation and acceptable noise levels
- Required workshop, parts, wash-down, fuel, and storage capacity
- Whether you will sell directly from the site or only demonstrate equipment

Have a civil engineer or site designer prepare a concept plan based on your actual inventory. The key measurements should come from the largest combination you expect to run, not your current smallest machine.

## 2. Suggested allocation of the 11 hectares

A practical initial layout might look like this:

| Area | Approximate allocation | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|
| Entrance, parking, visitor circulation | 0.5–1.0 ha | Customer vehicles, trailers, accessible parking |
| Workshop and hardstand | 0.5–1.0 ha | Repairs, preparation, loading, staging |
| Demonstration loop and test lanes | 2–3 ha | Tractors, loaders, transport demonstrations |
| Working field plots | 3–4 ha | Tillage, planting, mowing, harvesting demonstrations |
| Storage and overflow inventory | 1–2 ha | Machinery awaiting preparation or sale |
| Drainage, buffers, landscaping, future expansion | 1–2 ha | Swales, ponds, screening, setbacks, reserve capacity |

Do not pave the whole property. A combination of compacted aggregate, reinforced grass, and selected concrete or asphalt will usually be more economical and more authentic for farm machinery demonstrations.

## 3. Phase 1: planning, permissions, and surveys

Complete this before committing to earthworks.

### Confirm land-use permissions

Ownership does not automatically authorize commercial demonstrations. Check:

- Zoning and permitted commercial or agricultural uses
- Planning permission for customer visits and events
- Access and highway requirements
- Building permits
- Fire-code requirements
- Noise restrictions
- Signage restrictions
- Operating-hour limitations
- Environmental or watercourse protections
- Septic, well, or public utility approvals
- Fuel-storage and hazardous-material rules
- Stormwater and soil-disturbance permits

Your proposed use may be classified as machinery sales, agricultural service, equipment rental, vehicle testing, or an event venue depending on local rules.

### Order the basic surveys

Obtain:

- Boundary and topographic survey
- Soil and bearing-capacity testing
- Drainage and flood-risk assessment
- Utility-location survey
- Access and sight-line assessment
- Environmental review, especially if there are streams, wetlands, wells, or protected habitat

The flatness of the property is helpful, but flat ground can have poor drainage. Do not assume it needs little grading.

### Obtain insurance advice early

Ask your insurer about:

- Premises liability
- Product liability
- Demonstration and test-drive coverage
- Customer operation of equipment
- Employee operation
- Fire and theft
- Pollution or fuel-spill liability
- Event coverage
- Business interruption

If customers will operate equipment, use written waivers and a formal qualification process, but do not treat a waiver as a substitute for safe design and proper insurance.

## 4. Phase 2: site access, drainage, and utilities

These are the items most difficult to correct later.

### Entrance and internal circulation

Create one obvious entrance with:

- Adequate sight distance in both directions
- A gate set back far enough to prevent queuing onto the road
- Separate customer and delivery access if possible
- A truck-capable entrance apron
- Secure fencing and a lockable gate
- Clear signs for visitors, deliveries, and emergencies

Inside the site, use a **one-way circulation pattern** wherever possible. Keep customer cars away from machine loading, fuel storage, and workshop traffic.

### Drainage

Use a combination of:

- Shallow swales
- Crowned or cross-fall roads
- Culverts at crossings
- Vegetated drainage strips
- A detention or settlement pond where needed
- Stabilized outfalls

Keep clean roof water separate from contaminated workshop or wash-bay water. During construction, install erosion and sediment controls before stripping or grading the field.

### Utilities

Plan service capacity for:

- Three-phase power if you will use welders, compressors, chargers, or large workshop equipment
- Potable water
- Wash-bay water
- Sanitary facilities
- Internet and security systems
- Exterior lighting
- Emergency power or generator connection

If extending utilities is expensive, start with a smaller office/workshop building and make provisions for later expansion.

## 5. Phase 3: build the core hardstand and workshop

Your first construction package should support both operations and demonstrations.

### Main hardstand

Install a durable, well-drained hardstand near the workshop for:

- Incoming inspections
- Repairs and servicing
- Photographing inventory
- Customer walk-arounds
- Machine loading
- Short-term staging

Use reinforced concrete in areas exposed to hydraulic oil, fuel, heavy loading, or repeated turning. Compacted crushed stone may be adequate for general parking and storage if it is properly designed and maintained.

### Workshop

For two full-time mechanics, a sensible initial workshop would generally include:

- Two or more service bays
- At least one bay sized for your largest tractor and implement
- A high-clearance door
- Lifting and jacking equipment rated for your machinery
- Parts storage
- Clean and dirty work zones
- Compressed air
- Welding and fabrication area
- Battery charging area
- Fire separation and extinguishers
- Lockable tool and hazardous-material storage

Design vehicle access so a machine does not have to reverse through customer areas to reach the workshop.

### Fuel and fluids

Provide a dedicated, compliant area for:

- Diesel and gasoline, if used
- Lubricants
- Hydraulic oil
- Used oil
- Filters and contaminated absorbents
- DEF or other machine fluids

Use secondary containment, impact protection, spill kits, and appropriate fire protection. Do not place tanks beside a drainage swale, watercourse, or customer parking area.

## 6. Phase 4: build the demonstration areas

Use several types of demonstration space instead of one oversized field.

### A. Demonstration loop

Construct a loop wide enough for your largest expected machine combination, with:

- A straight section for transport and acceleration
- A broad turning area
- A slower technical section
- A separate pull-off or breakdown bay
- Good visibility from spectator areas
- A surface that remains usable after moderate rain

As a starting concept, consider a loop approximately **8–10 metres wide**, but size the width and turning areas from actual machine dimensions. Articulated loaders, combines, and long implement combinations may require much more space than a tractor alone.

### B. Straight test lane

A straight lane is useful for demonstrating:

- Road speed and braking
- Loader cycles
- Balers
- Mowers
- Sprayers
- Transport stability
- Noise and vibration

Keep it separate from public walking routes and provide a safe stopping area beyond the demonstration zone.

### C. Working field plots

Divide the working area into plots so you can demonstrate different functions without destroying the entire field:

- Tillage plot
- Seedbed or planting plot
- Grass or forage plot
- Rough-ground plot
- Mowing or residue-management plot
- Optional slope or traction area, if safe and permitted

Rotate use of the plots to prevent compaction. Avoid demonstrations on wet ground unless the machine is specifically being shown under those conditions and the risk is controlled.

### D. Loader and handling area

Create a dedicated area for:

- Buckets
- Forks
- Bale handling
- Pallet work
- Trailer loading
- Material movement

This should have a hard, level surface and should be completely separated from spectators. Never mix loader demonstrations with customer walking routes.

### E. Customer viewing area

Provide fixed areas where customers can stand safely:

- Raised or fenced viewing zone
- Shade or shelter
- Seating
- Clear sightlines
- No crossing of active machine paths
- Accessible route from parking
- Nearby toilets and hand-washing facilities

Avoid inviting customers to stand along the edge of an operating field with no physical separation.

## 7. Safety and operating rules

Write the site rules before opening.

### Minimum controls

- One-way vehicle routes where feasible
- Separate pedestrian paths
- Physical barriers around active demonstration areas
- Marked exclusion zones
- Speed limits
- High-visibility clothing for staff
- Dedicated spotters for reversing and tight maneuvers
- No unapproved passenger riding
- Lockout/tagout procedures for repairs
- Daily pre-start machine inspections
- Radios or reliable communications
- First-aid equipment and trained personnel
- Fire extinguishers and emergency shutdown procedures
- Clearly posted emergency address and access route
- Incident and near-miss reporting

### Customer operation

If buyers may drive machines, use a controlled process:

1. Verify license, age, and relevant experience.
2. Provide a briefing on the specific machine.
3. Restrict operation to an approved route.
4. Keep an employee in direct supervision.
5. Prohibit passengers unless the machine is designed and insured for them.
6. Stop operations in poor visibility, lightning, excessive wind, or unsafe ground conditions.
7. Record who operated what machine and when.

A demonstration ride with a salesperson driving is materially easier to control than allowing every visitor to operate equipment.

## 8. Environmental and neighbor considerations

A working yard can create more neighborhood friction through noise, dust, lighting, and traffic than through the machinery itself.

Plan for:

- Tree or hedge screening along boundaries
- Dust suppression on aggregate roads
- Restricted operating hours
- Downward-directed lighting
- No unnecessary idling
- Noise-sensitive scheduling
- Covered storage for scrap and parts
- Proper disposal of used oil, filters, tires, batteries, and contaminated soil
- A contained wash bay with approved wastewater treatment or disposal
- Spill response procedures
- Vegetated buffers near ditches and watercourses

Notify nearby residents before major construction and establish a contact number for concerns. A professional, predictable operating schedule often prevents disputes.

## 9. Customer facilities and presentation

Buyers do not need a luxury dealership, but the site should communicate control and credibility.

Include:

- Clearly marked entrance
- Reception or small sales office
- Clean toilets
- Drinking water
- Covered briefing area
- Machine information boards
- Wi-Fi or reliable mobile connectivity
- Good site lighting
- Security cameras and gated access
- Professional signage
- A clean photography area for listings

Have machines washed, fueled, inspected, and arranged before customers arrive. A well-run demonstration yard can become a major sales asset even if the buildings are modest.

## 10. Recommended implementation sequence

### Stage 1 — 0 to 3 months
- Confirm zoning and approvals
- Survey and test soils
- Prepare concept and drainage plan
- Obtain insurance and contractor pricing
- Choose the first machines and demonstrations the yard must support

### Stage 2 — 3 to 6 months
- Secure access and fencing
- Install drainage and utilities
- Construct the entrance, primary hardstand, and basic parking
- Build or adapt the workshop
- Establish temporary customer facilities if necessary

### Stage 3 — 6 to 9 months
- Construct the demonstration loop
- Install viewing barriers and pedestrian routes
- Develop one or two working plots
- Add fuel, wash-down, lighting, signage, and security systems

### Stage 4 — 9 to 12 months
- Trial the site with staff only
- Run emergency and breakdown drills
- Invite a few trusted repeat buyers
- Correct traffic-flow, drainage, and safety problems
- Launch scheduled demonstrations

### Stage 5 — Year 2
- Add more field plots
- Expand hardstand and storage
- Add shelter, office, or training space
- Improve landscaping and screening
- Host larger field days only after the basic operation is proven

## 11. Budget structure

Local prices vary too much for a reliable total without a survey and site plan, but divide the budget into these packages:

1. Planning, surveys, engineering, and permits  
2. Access road and entrance works  
3. Grading, drainage, and erosion control  
4. Aggregate and concrete hardstand  
5. Workshop and office  
6. Utilities and sanitation  
7. Demonstration track and field improvements  
8. Fencing, gates, barriers, and signage  
9. Fuel, wash bay, and environmental controls  
10. Lighting, security, and communications  
11. Insurance, legal, and opening costs  
12. Contingency—often at least 15% for a first earthworks project

The expensive mistakes are usually poor drainage, undersized access, insufficient turning space, and building customer routes through operating areas.

## 12. A sensible minimum viable opening

You do not need to complete all 11 hectares before opening. A strong first version could consist of:

- Approved commercial/agricultural use
- Safe entrance and fenced perimeter
- Workshop and service hardstand
- Customer parking and toilets
- One all-weather demonstration loop
- One working field plot
- Viewing area and pedestrian route
- Fuel and spill-control arrangements
- Written operating and emergency procedures
- Proper insurance

That gives you a professional, independent venue while preserving most of the property for future expansion and additional demonstration activities.

Below is a model bill written for adaptation to a particular jurisdiction. Bracketed terms should be replaced with the relevant statutory citations, document classes, agencies, fees, and dates. It is structured to end an exclusive charter while preserving the legal reliability of existing records and creating an open, government-operated registry.

---

# A BILL

## To repeal the exclusive statutory authentication franchise held by [NAME OF ASSOCIATION], establish an open public registry for the authentication and verification of [COVERED DOCUMENTS], provide for the transition of existing records and pending matters, and for related purposes.

### Be it enacted by the [Legislature/Parliament] of [JURISDICTION]:

## Section 1. Short title.

This Act may be cited as the **Open Official Document Authentication and Public Registry Act**.

## Section 2. Legislative findings and purposes.

The [Legislature] finds that:

1. Certain official documents are presently required by law to bear the authentication, seal, or certification of [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] or its members before those documents are legally effective.

2. The exclusive statutory authority granted to [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] constitutes a closed professional monopoly over a public authentication function.

3. Authentication of official documents is a governmental recordkeeping and verification function that should be available on equal terms to all persons through an open, transparent, and accountable public system.

4. An open public registry can reduce unnecessary costs, improve access, provide uniform standards, preserve reliable records, and permit independent verification.

5. The transition to an open registry should not invalidate documents previously authenticated in accordance with law, impair vested rights, or disrupt pending proceedings.

The purposes of this Act are to:

1. End the exclusive statutory authentication authority of [NAME OF ASSOCIATION];

2. Establish the [NAME OF REGISTRY] as the official public system for recording and verifying covered documents;

3. Permit any person to submit an eligible document or authentication request directly to the Registry;

4. Establish uniform, technology-neutral standards for authentication, verification, correction, retention, and public access; and

5. Maintain the integrity, security, privacy, and evidentiary value of official records.

## Section 3. Definitions.

For purposes of this Act:

(a) **“Agency”** means the [Department/Ministry/Office] designated under Section 7.

(b) **“Authentication”** means the official confirmation, based on the records and procedures prescribed by this Act, of:

   (1) the identity or authority of the issuing public body or authorized official;

   (2) the integrity of the document or certified copy submitted;

   (3) the date and time of issuance, filing, or verification; and

   (4) any additional fact expressly required by law for the document to be recognized as authentic.

Authentication does not constitute a finding that every factual assertion within a document is true unless another law expressly provides otherwise.

(c) **“Covered document”** means a document within the class currently subject to authentication under [CITATION TO CURRENT LAW], including any document later designated by the Agency pursuant to Section 16.

(d) **“Document”** includes a paper record, electronic record, certified copy, digital file, image, data record, or other recorded information capable of being retained and reproduced.

(e) **“Registry”** means the [NAME OF REGISTRY] established under Section 7.

(f) **“Registry certificate”** means an electronic or paper certificate issued by the Registry stating that a covered document has been recorded or authenticated in accordance with this Act.

(g) **“Submitting person”** means any natural person, legal entity, public body, or authorized representative that submits a document or request to the Registry.

(h) **“Legacy authentication”** means an authentication, seal, certificate, or certification issued by [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] or one of its members before the effective date of this Act.

## Section 4. Termination of exclusive authentication franchise.

(a) Notwithstanding any other law, on and after the effective date of this Act, [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] and its members shall have no exclusive right, franchise, privilege, or statutory authority to authenticate a covered document.

(b) No law, charter, regulation, contract, or other instrument shall be construed to require a covered document to bear the seal, stamp, signature, approval, or certification of [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] or its members, except as expressly provided for legacy documents under Section 12.

(c) A covered document shall not be denied legal effect solely because it lacks the seal, stamp, signature, or certification of [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] or its members if the document has been authenticated or recorded in accordance with this Act.

(d) [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] may continue to operate as a voluntary professional or trade association, but it shall not exercise governmental, exclusive, or compulsory authority under the laws of this jurisdiction.

## Section 5. Recognition of Registry authentication.

(a) A covered document authenticated by the Registry in accordance with this Act shall be legally sufficient for every purpose for which authentication by [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] was required under any law, unless a specific statute expressly requires an additional and separate act.

(b) A Registry certificate, whether issued electronically or in paper form, shall be prima facie evidence of:

   (1) the identity of the Registry;

   (2) the date and time of authentication or filing;

   (3) the integrity of the associated document or record; and

   (4) the facts stated in the certificate.

(c) A person relying in good faith on a Registry certificate shall not be liable solely because the certificate was later corrected, suspended, or withdrawn, unless the person knew or reasonably should have known that the certificate was fraudulent or invalid.

(d) The Registry may use electronic signatures, seals, verification codes, cryptographic hashes, digital certificates, distributed verification methods, or other reliable technologies. No particular technology shall be required if the authentication method provides equivalent security and verifiability.

## Section 6. Direct public access and submissions.

(a) Any person may submit a covered document or request authentication directly to the Registry, subject only to:

   (1) applicable filing requirements;

   (2) reasonable identity or authority verification;

   (3) payment of a fee authorized under Section 14; and

   (4) compliance with lawful privacy, confidentiality, and security requirements.

(b) The Registry shall not require a submitting person to obtain the approval, sponsorship, referral, or intermediation of [NAME OF ASSOCIATION], a member of that association, or any other private organization.

(c) The Registry shall accept submissions through reasonably accessible methods, including:

   (1) an online portal;

   (2) in-person submission; and

   (3) mail or another method approved by the Agency for persons unable to use the online portal.

(d) The Registry shall provide reasonable assistance to persons with disabilities, persons lacking reliable internet access, and persons requiring language assistance.

(e) Submission of a document shall not by itself establish the truth of disputed factual statements contained in the document, and the Registry shall not be required to adjudicate matters outside its statutory authority.

## Section 7. Establishment and administration of Registry.

(a) There is established within the [AGENCY] a public system to be known as the **[NAME OF REGISTRY]**.

(b) The Agency shall administer the Registry and shall be responsible for:

   (1) receiving and processing submissions;

   (2) authenticating and recording covered documents;

   (3) issuing Registry certificates;

   (4) maintaining an index sufficient for public verification;

   (5) preserving records in a secure and durable manner;

   (6) investigating suspected fraud or misuse;

   (7) publishing standards, procedures, and service levels; and

   (8) reporting annually to the [Legislature/Minister/Parliament] on the operation of the Registry.

(c) The Agency may enter into agreements with other public bodies for the verification of issuing authorities, source records, identity information, or other matters necessary to administer the Registry.

(d) The Agency may contract for technical services, provided that:

   (1) the Agency retains legal responsibility for the Registry;

   (2) public records remain subject to applicable access, retention, audit, and security laws; and

   (3) no contractor receives an exclusive statutory right to authenticate covered documents.

## Section 8. Authentication procedure.

(a) Upon receiving a submission, the Registry shall determine whether:

   (1) the document is within the covered class;

   (2) the submitting person has authority to submit it, where authority is required;

   (3) the issuing body or official can be verified;

   (4) the document is complete and legible;

   (5) the document has been altered, corrupted, or previously recorded in a manner requiring review; and

   (6) any other requirement prescribed by this Act or regulation has been satisfied.

(b) If the requirements are satisfied, the Registry shall authenticate or record the document and issue a Registry certificate.

(c) If the Registry determines that a submission is deficient, it shall provide the submitting person with written notice stating:

   (1) the reason for the deficiency;

   (2) the information or correction required; and

   (3) the procedure and deadline for resubmission or review.

(d) The Registry shall act on a complete submission within [NUMBER] business days, except where additional verification is reasonably necessary.

(e) The Agency shall publish objective standards for determining whether a submission is complete and whether additional verification is required.

## Section 9. Public verification.

(a) The Registry shall provide a publicly accessible method for verifying a Registry certificate, subject to this Act and applicable privacy law.

(b) The verification system shall permit a person to determine at least:

   (1) whether a certificate was issued;

   (2) the date of issuance;

   (3) the issuing authority or source identified in the certificate;

   (4) whether the certificate is active, corrected, suspended, or withdrawn; and

   (5) whether the document associated with the certificate has been altered or superseded.

(c) The Agency may restrict public access to the contents of a document when disclosure would violate privacy, confidentiality, national security, personal safety, or another express legal protection. In such cases, the Registry shall provide the maximum lawful verification information without disclosing protected content.

(d) The Agency shall maintain an audit trail showing material actions taken with respect to each Registry record.

## Section 10. Corrections, suspension, and withdrawal.

(a) The Registry may correct a clerical, technical, or administrative error in a record.

(b) The Registry may suspend or withdraw a Registry certificate if it has reasonable grounds to believe that:

   (1) the certificate was obtained through fraud, material misrepresentation, or unauthorized submission;

   (2) the underlying document was forged, materially altered, or unlawfully issued;

   (3) the certificate was issued in error; or

   (4) continued recognition would create a substantial risk of harm or undermine the integrity of the Registry.

(c) Except where immediate action is necessary to prevent fraud or imminent harm, the Registry shall provide notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond before suspending or withdrawing a certificate.

(d) A decision under this section shall be in writing and shall state the reasons for the decision.

(e) A person adversely affected by a decision under this section may request administrative review within [NUMBER] days. The Agency shall establish procedures for prompt review and, where appropriate, judicial appeal under [ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURE LAW].

(f) Correction, suspension, or withdrawal shall not automatically invalidate a transaction or legal act completed in good-faith reliance on the certificate before notice of the action, except as otherwise provided by law.

## Section 11. Offenses and enforcement.

(a) A person commits an offense if the person knowingly:

   (1) submits a forged, materially altered, or fraudulent document;

   (2) impersonates the Registry or an officer or employee of the Registry;

   (3) creates or uses a counterfeit Registry certificate, seal, verification code, or electronic credential;

   (4) knowingly alters a Registry record without authorization; or

   (5) falsely represents that [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] or its members retain exclusive statutory authority under this Act.

(b) A violation of this section shall be subject to the penalties provided by [APPLICABLE FRAUD, FORGERY, COMPUTER MISUSE, OR PUBLIC RECORDS LAW].

(c) Nothing in this section shall impose criminal liability for an honest mistake, technical defect, or good-faith submission corrected through the procedures established by the Agency.

## Section 12. Legacy documents and transition.

(a) A legacy authentication issued before the effective date of this Act remains valid and legally effective to the same extent as if this Act had not been enacted.

(b) A document pending before [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] on the effective date shall, at the option of the submitting person:

   (1) be completed under the law in effect before the effective date; or

   (2) be transferred to the Registry without requiring a new submission fee, except for a fee expressly authorized for additional services.

(c) [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] shall, within [NUMBER] days after the effective date, transfer to the Agency all public records, indexes, authentication logs, and other materials reasonably necessary to preserve continuity of official verification.

(d) The transfer required by this section shall be conducted in a secure and orderly manner and shall preserve the evidentiary status, original metadata, and chain of custody of transferred records.

(e) Nothing in this Act shall:

   (1) retroactively invalidate a document properly authenticated before the effective date;

   (2) extinguish a claim, defense, or proceeding based solely on the change in authentication system; or

   (3) require a person to reauthenticate a document solely because the exclusive franchise has ended.

(f) During the transition period, which shall not exceed [12/18] months after the effective date, the Agency may accept legacy authentication records for purposes of verification and may issue replacement Registry certificates without requiring reauthentication of the underlying document.

## Section 13. Records, privacy, and security.

(a) Registry records are public records except to the extent that access is restricted by this Act or another law protecting confidential or personal information.

(b) The Agency shall adopt safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of Registry information, including:

   (1) access controls;

   (2) authentication of Registry personnel;

   (3) encryption where appropriate;

   (4) backup and disaster-recovery procedures;

   (5) tamper-evident audit logs; and

   (6) periodic independent security assessments.

(c) The Agency shall retain Registry records for at least [NUMBER] years or for the period required by the applicable public-records retention schedule, whichever is longer.

(d) The Agency shall publish a privacy policy describing:

   (1) information collected;

   (2) purposes of collection;

   (3) retention periods;

   (4) permitted disclosures;

   (5) correction procedures; and

   (6) procedures for reporting unauthorized access or disclosure.

## Section 14. Fees and financial administration.

(a) The Agency may charge reasonable fees for authentication, certification, copies, expedited service, and other services directly provided by the Registry.

(b) Fees shall be established by regulation and shall be limited to the reasonable cost of administering the Registry, preserving records, maintaining security, and providing requested services.

(c) The Agency shall provide fee waivers or reductions for:

   (1) indigent persons;

   (2) public bodies acting in an official capacity;

   (3) documents required for access to public benefits or legal rights; and

   (4) other categories established by regulation.

(d) Fees shall not be structured to create an exclusive commercial advantage for any private association or intermediary.

(e) All fees collected under this section shall be deposited into [GENERAL FUND/SPECIAL REGISTRY FUND] and used for the purposes authorized by this Act.

## Section 15. Personnel and professional transition.

(a) Nothing in this Act prevents a former member, employee, or contractor of [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] from applying for employment or contracting opportunities with the Agency, subject to ordinary public-service requirements.

(b) The Agency may establish training, certification, and qualification standards for Registry officers and employees.

(c) No person shall be required to belong to [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] or any other private organization as a condition of employment, appointment, contracting, or access to Registry services.

(d) This Act does not prohibit private persons from offering document-preparation, legal, translation, courier, or other services, provided that no person falsely represents that private services are required for Registry authentication.

## Section 16. Regulations and standards.

(a) Within [180] days after enactment, the Agency shall issue proposed regulations necessary to implement this Act.

(b) Regulations shall address, at a minimum:

   (1) submission formats and procedures;

   (2) identity and authority verification;

   (3) electronic signatures and seals;

   (4) standards for certified copies and translations;

   (5) record retention and archival preservation;

   (6) fees and fee waivers;

   (7) privacy and restricted-access records;

   (8) correction, suspension, withdrawal, and appeal procedures;

   (9) accessibility and language assistance; and

   (10) interoperability with other public registries.

(c) Before adopting final regulations, the Agency shall publish them for public comment and consult with public bodies, courts, affected professionals, civil-society organizations, accessibility advocates, privacy experts, and technology-security experts.

(d) Regulations shall not restore or create an exclusive authentication right in favor of [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] or any other private organization.

## Section 17. Repeals and conforming amendments.

(a) The following provisions are repealed:

   (1) [CITATION granting exclusive authentication authority to NAME OF ASSOCIATION];

   (2) [CITATION requiring the seal, stamp, or certification of NAME OF ASSOCIATION];

   (3) [CITATION establishing compulsory membership or payment as a condition of authentication]; and

   (4) any provision inconsistent with this Act.

(b) Each reference in [LIST OF STATUTES] to authentication by [NAME OF ASSOCIATION] shall be replaced with a reference to authentication by the [NAME OF REGISTRY] or, where applicable, a Registry certificate.

(c) The [LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL/LAW REVISION OFFICE] shall prepare any additional technical amendments necessary to conform the code to this Act.

## Section 18. Report to the [Legislature/Parliament].

Beginning one year after the effective date, and annually for the next four years, the Agency shall submit a report containing:

1. The number and type of submissions received;

2. Processing times and rejection rates;

3. Fees collected and operating costs;

4. Complaints, corrections, suspensions, withdrawals, and appeals;

5. Security incidents and remedial actions;

6. Accessibility and service-delivery data;

7. The status of the transfer of legacy records; and

8. Recommendations for improving the Registry.

## Section 19. No private right to exclusive authentication.

No private organization, association, licensee, or other person has a vested or continuing right to perform the governmental authentication function established by this Act on an exclusive basis.

Nothing in this section shall be construed to:

1. impair a valid contract unrelated to an exclusive statutory authentication right;

2. deny compensation otherwise required by the constitution or laws of this jurisdiction; or

3. prevent a person from seeking judicial review of an action taken under this Act.

## Section 20. Severability.

If any provision of this Act, or its application to any person or circumstance, is held invalid, the invalidity shall not affect the remaining provisions or applications of the Act that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application.

## Section 21. Effective date.

(a) Sections 4, 5, 6, 11, 12, 17, and 19 shall take effect on [DATE].

(b) The Agency shall begin accepting submissions through the Registry no later than [DATE], and in no event later than [180] days after enactment.

(c) The remaining provisions shall take effect upon enactment or on the dates otherwise specified in this Act.

## Optional sponsor’s statement

This bill replaces a closed statutory authentication franchise with an open, public, and accountable system. It does not eliminate authentication; it moves authentication from a private monopoly into a government-operated registry available directly to the public. The bill protects documents already authenticated, provides a transition for pending matters, preserves privacy and evidentiary reliability, and establishes transparent procedures for verification, correction, appeal, and public oversight.

Before circulation, the proposal should be conformed to the jurisdiction’s constitution, administrative-procedure requirements, public-records and privacy laws, government-employee rules, fee restrictions, procurement law, and any applicable compensation or takings provisions.

# 3. Syllabus outline

## Course title

**Budget Analysis for Public-Sector Decision-Makers**

## Learning outcomes

By the end of the course, participants should be able to:

1. Explain the main stages of the public-budget cycle.
2. Distinguish between recurrent, capital, statutory, discretionary, and contingent expenditure.
3. Read and interrogate a departmental budget.
4. Test the assumptions behind spending proposals.
5. Analyse variances between approved, revised, and actual expenditure.
6. Assess affordability over the medium term.
7. Identify fiscal, delivery, and implementation risks.
8. Use basic scenario and sensitivity analysis.
9. Produce a concise recommendation for a senior official or budget committee.
10. Communicate financial analysis clearly to non-specialists.

---

## Day One: Understanding and interrogating the budget

### Module 1: The budget as a policy and management instrument

**Topics**

- What a public budget is designed to achieve
- The relationship between policy, planning, budgeting, and delivery
- Annual budgets and medium-term expenditure frameworks
- Roles of ministries, departments, treasuries, finance units, and spending agencies
- The budget calendar and key decision points

**Practical exercise**

Participants map a typical budget proposal from policy idea to approval, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation.

---

### Module 2: Reading the structure of a public budget

**Topics**

- Revenue, expenditure, financing, and fiscal balance
- Administrative, economic, functional, and programme classifications
- Recurrent and capital expenditure
- Personnel, procurement, transfers, grants, and debt-service costs
- Gross versus net expenditure
- Voted, statutory, earmarked, and externally financed spending

**Practical exercise**

Participants classify a set of budget lines and identify what each classification reveals—or conceals.

---

### Module 3: From appropriations to actual spending

**Topics**

- Approved budgets, in-year revisions, cash releases, commitments, and actual expenditure
- Budget execution rates
- Common causes of underspending and overspending
- Commitment controls and arrears
- Reallocations, supplementary estimates, and virements
- The difference between a low execution rate and a genuine saving

**Practical exercise**

Participants analyse a departmental expenditure report and prepare three questions for the responsible finance officer.

---

### Module 4: Testing the assumptions behind a proposal

**Topics**

- Volume, price, timing, and coverage assumptions
- Unit costs and demand forecasts
- Staffing and remuneration assumptions
- Inflation, exchange-rate, and interest-rate exposure
- Procurement and implementation assumptions
- One-off costs versus recurring costs
- Optimism bias and strategic understatement

**Practical exercise**

Participants review a fictional proposal for a public-service expansion and identify weak or unsupported assumptions.

---

## Day Two: Analysis, risk, and recommendations

### Module 5: Medium-term affordability

**Topics**

- Baseline budgets and new policy proposals
- Multi-year costing
- The future operating cost of capital projects
- Fixed, variable, and semi-variable costs
- Fiscal space and competing priorities
- Sustainability and recurring commitments
- Intergenerational and distributional considerations

**Practical exercise**

Participants build a three-year cost profile for a proposed programme.

---

### Module 6: Variance and performance analysis

**Topics**

- Budget-to-actual and year-on-year analysis
- Price, volume, timing, and mix variances
- Linking financial performance to service outputs
- Selecting meaningful indicators
- Avoiding misleading comparisons
- Distinguishing financial control problems from delivery problems

**Practical exercise**

Participants prepare a short variance commentary for a senior management report.

---

### Module 7: Scenario and sensitivity analysis

**Topics**

- Base case, upside case, and downside case
- Sensitivity to inflation, demand, exchange rates, and delivery delays
- Break-even analysis
- Contingency and reserve requirements
- Interpreting uncertainty without creating false precision
- Presenting scenarios to decision-makers

**Practical exercise**

Participants test a programme budget against three adverse scenarios and recommend mitigations.

---

### Module 8: Fiscal and implementation risk

**Topics**

- Identifying fiscal, operational, legal, procurement, and reputational risks
- Risk registers and risk ownership
- Contingent liabilities and guarantees
- Public-private partnerships and long-term commitments
- Procurement delays and implementation capacity
- Controls, assurance, and escalation

**Practical exercise**

Participants produce a risk table covering probability, impact, mitigation, and responsible owner.

---

### Module 9: Writing the decision note

**Topics**

- Turning analysis into a recommendation
- Writing for ministers, permanent secretaries, agency heads, and budget committees
- Separating facts, assumptions, judgements, and recommendations
- Presenting options rather than merely describing problems
- Using tables and charts effectively
- Common weaknesses in financial briefing papers

**Practical exercise**

Participants prepare a two-page decision note based on the case study.

---

## Final applied assessment

Participants complete a short case involving:

- A departmental spending proposal
- A three-year cost profile
- Budget execution data
- Several uncertain assumptions
- A requirement to recommend whether, and under what conditions, the proposal should proceed

Assessment criteria:

- Accuracy of analysis
- Identification of material assumptions
- Treatment of uncertainty
- Quality of recommendation
- Clarity of written presentation

Provide participants with:

- Budget glossary

- Multi-year costing template
- Variance-analysis template

You can build this into a legitimate revenue stream, but the first priority is to make the ownership and conflict-of-interest position unambiguous. A strong product can be undermined quickly if clients, your employer, or a public procurement authority later argues that it was developed using company resources or that your sales activity influenced public work.

## 1. Establish that you actually own the tool

Before marketing it, get advice from an IP/employment lawyer and review:

- Your employment agreement, invention-assignment clauses, confidentiality obligations, and outside-business rules.
- Whether you developed it on company time, equipment, accounts, or paid leave.
- Whether it uses employer-owned data, templates, code, standards libraries, client information, or internal methods.
- Whether it was created in connection with work you were hired to do.
- Whether your jurisdiction treats employee-created inventions or software as employer-owned even without a specific assignment.

Keep a dated development record and separate copies of genuinely personal materials. Do not move employer code or confidential project data into a new venture. If there is any ambiguity, seek a written carve-out or licence from the employer before investing heavily.

## 2. Separate the venture from your public-sector role

Because you work in engineering consulting and public reconstruction money is involved, put formal safeguards in place:

- Disclose the venture to your employer and obtain written approval for outside commercial activity.
- Do not use your employer’s client list, tender information, staff time, systems, brand, or confidential project knowledge.
- Do not sell to or influence decisions involving public entities where you have a professional or personal role.
- Do not participate in procurement, evaluation, specification-writing, or grant decisions that could benefit your tool or its customers.
- Avoid presenting yourself as acting for your employer unless formally authorised.
- Decline any arrangement that involves disguising personal compensation as project cost, steering public contracts, or using privileged information.

A useful rule is: if the arrangement would look improper when described in a procurement audit or newspaper article, do not do it.

## 3. Define the product narrowly

Do not begin with “a proprietary design tool.” Define one expensive, recurring problem it solves.

For example:

- Reduces design time for a specific class of reconstruction project.
- Automates compliance checking against a defined standard.
- Produces better cost, carbon, resilience, or constructability options.
- Reduces rework between engineering, architecture, and contractor teams.
- Creates an auditable decision trail that clients can use for approvals.

Write a one-page product brief:

1. Target customer.
2. Current workflow and pain point.
3. Quantified benefit.
4. What the tool does and does not do.
5. Required inputs and outputs.
6. Why an existing spreadsheet, CAD/BIM plug-in, or consultancy service is insufficient.
7. Evidence needed for a client to trust it.

The best initial customer is usually a private firm with a clear commercial incentive—not a public agency whose procurement process could create conflicts.

## 4. Validate willingness to pay before building a company around it

Over the next three to six months, conduct structured interviews with perhaps 15–25 potential buyers:

- Private developers.
- Contractors and design-build firms.
- Specialist engineering practices.
- Asset owners.
- Insurers, lenders, or project managers, if the tool affects risk or approvals.

Do not disclose confidential features or use sensitive current-project information. Ask about their present process, cost, decision-maker, procurement threshold, security concerns, and budget—not merely whether they “like the idea.”

Try to secure:

- Two or three paid discovery engagements.
- A pilot letter of intent.
- A customer willing to provide anonymized test data.
- Agreement on success metrics.

A paid pilot is much stronger evidence than positive feedback.

## 5. Choose a commercially simple first model

For a specialist engineering tool, possible models include:

### Annual licence
A firm pays for access, support, and updates. This is often easiest for a professional B2B product.

### Per-project licence
Useful if customers have irregular workloads, though it can make revenue less predictable.

### Seat or usage-based pricing
Appropriate if usage is measurable and customers vary substantially in size.

### Tool plus implementation
Charge separately for setup, training, integration, and support. Avoid allowing implementation work to obscure whether the underlying product is valuable.

### White-label or enterprise licence
Potentially lucrative, but it may give away too much control or create support obligations early.

A sensible starting point might be a paid pilot followed by an annual licence, with implementation priced separately. Avoid granting perpetual, unrestricted rights until you understand the product’s value and support burden.

## 6. Build a minimum commercially credible version

The first version does not need every feature. It does need:

- Reproducible outputs.
- Clear version control.
- Input validation and error handling.
- Documentation and training material.
- A method for checking results.
- Appropriate professional disclaimers.
- Data security suitable for the client’s environment.
- A reliable support and bug-reporting process.

If the tool produces engineering or safety-relevant outputs, determine whether it requires independent verification, professional sign-off, certification, or regulatory approval. Do not market it as replacing a licensed engineer’s judgement unless that is legally and technically supportable.

## 7. Protect the IP without overestimating it

Consider:

- Copyright protection for software and documentation.
- Trade-secret protection for algorithms, workflows, and data structures.
- A patent only if there is a genuinely novel, defensible technical invention and the economics justify it.
- A distinctive product name and trademark.
- Licence terms restricting copying, reverse engineering, sublicensing, and unauthorised use.
- Ownership rules for customer data, outputs, improvements, and integrations.

Do not publish enabling technical details before taking advice on patentability. In many cases, disciplined confidentiality and a defensible product advantage are more valuable than a speculative patent.

## 8. Create a clean commercial structure

Once validation is positive:

- Form a separate company if liability, ownership, or future investment justify it.
- Use a dedicated bank account, email domain, repository, cloud account, and accounting system.
- Put founder ownership and any collaborator contributions in writing.
- Use proper customer agreements covering licence scope, payment, support, warranties, liability caps, data protection, termination, and use of outputs.
- Obtain professional indemnity, cyber, and general business insurance as appropriate.
- Have an accountant advise on tax, VAT/sales tax, salary, dividends, and cross-border licensing.

Keep consulting services and software licensing distinct in contracts and invoices. That helps demonstrate what customers are actually paying for and makes the business easier to scale.

## 9. Plan around your employment

There are three realistic paths:

1. **Build part-time with approval**, while staying in your current role.
2. **Negotiate a formal spin-out or licence** with your employer if they have a legitimate claim or useful distribution capability.
3. **Leave and pursue it full-time** once revenue or committed contracts justify the risk.

Set objective transition criteria, such as:

- Three paying customers.
- Twelve months of credible contracted revenue.
- A repeatable sales process.
- Enough cash for 9–12 months of personal and business expenses.
- No unresolved ownership or conflict issue.

Do not assume a senior title is required to sell the product. Your current market credibility may help, but the product should eventually stand on customer results rather than your employer affiliation.

## A practical two-year sequence

### Months 0–3
- Review employment and IP documents.
- Obtain written internal clearance.
- Separate all personal development infrastructure.
- Interview potential buyers.
- Define one initial use case and a measurable value proposition.

### Months 4–6
- Build a minimum viable product.
- Run tests using clean, authorised data.
- Secure one or two paid pilots.
- Obtain legal review of the licence and pilot agreement.
- Establish the business entity if appropriate.

### Months 7–12
- Turn pilots into case studies with permission.
- Improve reliability, documentation, onboarding, and security.
- Set pricing based on measurable customer value.
- Close three to five paying customers.
- Track support time and gross margin carefully.

### Months 13–18
- Standardise implementation and training.
- Develop a repeatable sales channel through private-sector partners or specialist conferences.
- Add only features tied to customer demand.
- Hire contractors for product or support work where needed.
- Review whether your employment arrangement remains workable.

### Months 19–24
- Decide whether to remain part-time, negotiate a spin-out, or leave.
- Focus on recurring licence revenue rather than one-off custom work.
- Build renewal and expansion processes.
- Consider integrations, channel partners, or enterprise licensing.
- Keep public-sector opportunities ring-fenced unless the conflict position is independently cleared.

The central test is whether you can create a product that private customers voluntarily pay for, using clean IP, transparent contracts, and demonstrable value. If you do that, you are building durable personal wealth rather than merely extracting income from a temporary public spending cycle.
